title: Solving Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) via the Normal Equations
description: Augment X with a column of ones to form X_design, compute theta_star = np.linalg.inv(X_design.T @ X_design) @ (X_design.T @ y), and plot the fitted OLS line against the true noiseless line.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Prepend a column of ones to `X` (`X_design = np.c_[np.ones((n, 1)), X]`), compute `theta_star = np.linalg.inv(X_design.T @ X_design) @ (X_design.T @ y)`, unpack `theta0_star, theta1_star`, and print the estimated and true equations.

Evaluate `y_line_fit` and `y_line_true` over the supplied evenly spaced `x_line` positions from 0 to 2. Plot both lines on top of `plt.scatter(X[:, 0], y)` and print the closed-form MSE (`0.5162141209389142`).

Look at lines 3-4: `X_design` has one row per sample and 2 columns. Thus, `X_design.T @ X_design` is a `2 x 2` Gram matrix and `X_design.T @ y` is a 2-element vector. This gives the 2-element parameter vector `theta_star = [theta0_star, theta1_star]`.

steps.question: Why does `theta_star` (`theta0=5.172, theta1=2.816`) come out close to, but not exactly equal to, `theta0_true=5.000, theta1_true=3.000`?
steps.answer: The observed targets `y` include finite-sample Gaussian noise with the supplied standard deviation. Thus, the line that minimizes squared error on those noisy points is slightly shifted from the underlying noiseless line.
